steps.title: Four layers, later ones win
steps.body:
U-Boot's settings, such as `bootcmd`, `fdt_file`, `console` and `kernelargs`, are variables. Each can come from any of four layers, and the higher layer wins.

The panel on the right shows what this board actually did.

steps.title: 1. The default is baked into u-boot.bin
steps.body:
It comes from `board/variscite/imx8mp_var_dart/imx8mp_var_dart.env` and is always present. You can read the result in `build/deploy/u-boot-initial-env`.

It is used when nothing else exists.

steps.title: 2. A saved environment replaces layer 1 entirely
steps.body:
`saveenv` writes 16 KiB at 7 MiB on the boot device (`CONFIG_ENV_OFFSET = 0x700000`), protected by a CRC. If the CRC is valid it **replaces** the default completely, not just selected variables.

Reset it with `env default -a; saveenv`.

steps.title: 3. uEnv.txt overrides only what it lists
steps.body:
`bsp_bootcmd` imports this plain `name=value` file from partition 1 on every boot. For example `kernelargs=loglevel=8` changes just that one variable.

It is the safest way to experiment: delete the file to undo.

steps.title: 4. The prompt wins, until reset
steps.body:
Stop autoboot with any key, then use `setenv`, `printenv` and `run`. For example `setenv kernelargs quiet` followed by `boot`.

The change is lost on reset unless you `saveenv`.

steps.title: On this board only layer 1 was ever used
steps.body:
The first boot printed `bad CRC, using default environment`, so nothing was ever saved. Then `Failed to load '/boot/uEnv.txt'` shows there is no layer 3 either.

So every value came from the defaults this repository compiled. This is normal.

steps.anchor: Safest way to experiment: put one line in /boot/uEnv.txt (mount the card on your PC, or edit it on the board) and reboot. Delete the file to undo.
steps.title: Takeaway: experiment with one line in uEnv.txt
steps.body:
Mount the card on your PC or edit the file on the board, then reboot. If you broke a saved environment, stop autoboot and run `env default -a; saveenv; reset`.

From Linux, `fw_printenv` reads the variables.
